title: Where did it grow, and why there?

---
order: 1
unit: place
title: Where did it grow, and why there?
node: AC9HH7K09 n1
assumes: [AC9HH7K08]
summary: "Describe the landforms, rivers, climate and resources of the region where ancient China grew, and explain why the river valleys and plains could support many people while deserts and mountains could not. Geography is not a backdrop: each feature gave people something, or got in their way."
language: maths
hook: "Look at a map of China today and most people live in the east, on the plains and along the rivers. More than 2,000 years ago, it was much the same. Why there, and not out in the desert?"
---
An ancient society did not grow just anywhere. Historians start with the **physical geography** of the place: its **landforms** (plains, plateaus, mountains, deserts), its **waterways** (rivers, lakes, the sea), its **climate** (how hot, cold, wet or dry), and its **resources** (soil, wood, metal, salt).

Here is the land where the Qin and Han empires grew. It is a sketch, not an exact map.

![A schematic map of the Qin and Han heartland, not to scale: Gobi Desert and steppe in the north, Tibetan Plateau in the west, Loess Plateau, Yellow River, Wei River valley with the capitals, Qinling Mountains, North China Plain, Sichuan Basin, Yangtze River and the sea.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Feature | What it is like |
|---|---|
| Yellow River | Crosses the north. Its water is thick with fine yellow soil washed off the Loess Plateau, and when it floods it spreads that soil over the plain. |
| Loess Plateau | Deep, soft soil laid down by the wind. Easy to dig and farm with simple tools. |
| Wei River valley | A branch of the Yellow River, with mountains and passes around it. The Qin capital, and later the Han capital, were here. |
| North China Plain | Wide, flat land along the lower Yellow River. |
| Yangtze River | Crosses the south, where it is warmer and wetter. |
| Gobi Desert and steppe | Dry land to the north and north-west. Grassland herders, not farmers. |
| Tibetan Plateau and Qinling Mountains | High, rugged land to the west and south of the heartland. |

## Predict: why the river?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing first shows whether students reach for what the land gave people, or treat the location as chance."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Early farming villages in northern China grew up along the Yellow River and its branches, not out in the Gobi Desert. What is the most likely reason?"
  options:
    - "The rivers gave water and soft, rich soil for crops"
    - "The desert was too cold for anyone to live in"
    - "Villages near rivers were safe from floods"
    - "The emperor ordered people to live near the rivers"
  actual: "Water and soft, rich soil. Farming needs both, and the desert has neither. (Floods were a danger, not a safety, and farming villages there are thousands of years older than any emperor.)"
```

## Try: what did each feature give people?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Matching each feature to what it offered turns a list of place names into reasons people could live there."
check:
  type: match
  q: "Match each feature to what it gave people, or how it got in their way."
  pairs:
    - ["Yellow River", "Water, and fresh soil spread by its floods"]
    - ["Loess soil", "Soft ground that was easy to farm with simple tools"]
    - ["Mountains and passes around the Wei valley", "A heartland that was harder for enemies to reach"]
    - ["Gobi Desert and steppe", "Land too dry for farming villages"]
```

Was your guess right? Each feature either **gave people something** (water, soil, protection) or **got in their way** (too dry, too high, too far).

## Worked example: why the Wei River valley?

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Explaining why the Qin heartland worked, and catching Nib's 'it could have been anywhere', shows geography as a set of reasons, not scenery."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Historians often point out that the Wei River valley was a strong base for the state of Qin. Which reason uses the geography best?"
      options:
        - "It had river water, good farmland and mountains that slowed attackers"
        - "It was close to the sea, so the Qin could trade by ship"
        - "It was in the middle of the Gobi Desert, far from any enemies"
        - "It was the warmest and wettest part of China, so rice grew easily"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "Look at the map: the Wei valley is a long way inland. The sea is far to the east."
        - "The Gobi is to the north. The valley has a river, which the desert does not."
        - "That describes the Yangtze in the south. The Wei valley is cooler and drier."
      explain: "Farmland and water fed the people, and the mountains around the valley helped protect them. Both are reasons the place worked."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Nib is writing a map note (made up for this lesson). Click the first line where Nib's thinking goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: geography-is-backdrop
      explain: "Line 3: Nib treats the rivers and mountains as scenery that 'just happened' to be there. The water, soil and mountains are the reasons people could farm and defend the valley. Somewhere without them could not support the same cities."
    smaller:
      check:
        type: question
        q: "Could a farming village of the time have grown just as well in the middle of the dry Gobi Desert as beside the Yellow River?"
        options:
          - "No, because the desert has no river water or farm soil"
          - "Yes, because people can live anywhere if they work hard"
          - "Yes, because the desert had no floods to worry about"
          - "No, because the emperor did not allow it"
        answer: 0
        feedback:
          - null
          - "Hard work does not make water or soil appear. Farming needs both."
          - "No floods, but no water either. Crops would not grow."
          - "Rules are not the reason here. The land itself could not feed a village."
        explain: "Where people could farm depended on what the land gave them."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which feature mainly helped with defence rather than farming?"
      options:
        - "The Qinling Mountains south of the Wei valley"
        - "The yellow soil carried by the Yellow River"
        - "The soft loess soil of the plateau"
        - "The warm, wet weather along the Yangtze"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "The soil in the river helps crops. That is farming, not defence."
        - "Soft soil makes digging and planting easier. That is farming."
        - "Warm, wet weather helps rice grow. That is farming."
      explain: "Mountains made a barrier that attackers had to cross. Soil, silt and rain help crops grow."
```

### Farming or defence?

## Vary: north and south

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Changing the region shows that climate, not only rivers, shaped how people farmed."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Farmers on the Yellow River plains mostly grew millet, while farmers along the Yangtze mostly grew rice. Which best explains the difference?"
  options:
    - "The north is cooler and drier, and the south is warmer and wetter, which suits rice"
    - "The whole of China had the same climate, so the farmers just chose different crops"
    - "Rice needs dry, dusty soil, which the Yangtze had more of"
    - "Millet only grows where there are no rivers at all"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "Look at the map labels: the north and south have different climates."
    - "Rice usually grows in wet, flooded fields, not dry soil."
    - "The millet fields were along the Yellow River, so it does grow near rivers."
  explain: "Different climates suit different crops. Millet copes with the drier north; rice needs the warmer, wetter south."
```

## Practise: farming or barrier?

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Sorting features by what they mainly did checks that students can read a whole map for reasons."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Sort each feature by what it mainly did for people in the Qin and Han heartland."
  options: ["Mainly helped farming", "Mainly a barrier"]
  items:
    - ["Water from the Yellow River and its branches", "Mainly helped farming", "Rivers water the fields."]
    - ["Soft loess soil", "Mainly helped farming", "Easy to dig and plant."]
    - ["The dry Gobi Desert", "Mainly a barrier", "Too dry to farm, and hard to cross."]
    - ["The Qinling Mountains", "Mainly a barrier", "High land that blocks easy travel and attack."]
    - ["The high Tibetan Plateau", "Mainly a barrier", "Very high and cold, so hard to travel across or farm."]
    - ["Flat land on the North China Plain", "Mainly helped farming", "Wide, flat fields along the river."]
```

## Make: map the reasons in your book

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing about three features in their own book makes the link between land and settlement their own."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In my own book I chose a society (ancient China, or the one our class is studying), named three features of its land, wrote what each one gave people or how it got in their way, and wrote one sentence on why people could settle there. A partner read it and gave feedback." }
```

Write it in your own book or document, not on this page. Your partner or teacher reads it.

## Typical: the Nile

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "The same questions work on another river society, so the skill moves with the student."
check:
  type: question
  q: "In ancient Egypt, almost everyone lived in a narrow strip of land along the Nile. Which reason uses the geography best? (See the Egypt card on the Reference page.)"
  options:
    - "Desert lay on both sides, and the Nile's flood left soil and water"
    - "The river was the only place cool enough to live in the heat"
    - "The desert was full of cities already, so there was no room left"
    - "People lived by the river mainly to be near the sea for trade"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "Egypt's river valley is hot too. The difference is water and soil, not temperature."
    - "The desert was largely empty because it could not be farmed."
    - "Much of the Nile valley is a long way from the sea. The river itself was the draw."
  explain: "Like the Yellow River, the Nile gave water and fresh soil, and the land beyond it could not be farmed."
```

## Wider: mountains and sea in Greece

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "A society with little river farmland shows that the same questions can give a very different answer."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Ancient Greece had many separate city-states rather than one big river kingdom. How did its geography help make that so? (See the Greece card.)"
  options:
    - "Mountains split it into small valleys, and the sea linked them by boat"
    - "Greece had one huge river plain, so everyone lived in the same place"
    - "The sea kept the Greeks from ever meeting or trading with each other"
    - "Greece was a desert, so people had to live in tiny scattered groups"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "Greece had small valleys and plains, not one great river plain like the Yellow River or the Nile."
    - "The sea was how many Greeks travelled and traded with one another."
    - "Greece has dry summers, but it is not a desert. Mountains are the main reason."
  explain: "Geography does not decide everything, but it helps explain why Greece's communities were small and separate, and why the sea mattered so much."
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
learning: describe the landforms, waterways, climate and resources of ancient
  China's heartland and explain why people could settle there
summary: Describe the landforms, rivers, climate and resources of the region
  where ancient China grew, and explain why the river valleys and plains could
  support many people while deserts and mountains could not.
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 5 min · Practise 6
  min · Make 8 min. Typical and wider steps are extras and not counted in this.
goals:
  - I can name the main landforms, rivers and climate of the place an ancient
    society grew.
  - I can say what each feature gave people, or how it got in their way.
  - I can explain why people could settle in a place, using its geography.
struggle: Students list place names without saying what they did for people. Ask
  'so what did that give them?' after every feature.
before: >-
  This is the first hinge of AC9HH7K09: without a concrete picture of the place,
  the next two lessons (surplus, then opportunities and constraints) have
  nothing to reason from. The map is a schematic sketch (labelled so on the
  picture), not an accurate map; use an atlas or your textbook's map beside it
  if you have one.


  Usually Year 7; not yet tried with a class. The untiered path is the minimum.
  Time and optional width are the teacher's choices. No board or clips.


  Ancient China in the Qin and Han period is the worked example because many
  Year 7 classes study it. It is a model, not a requirement: the Reference page
  has short swap-in cards for Egypt, Greece, Rome and India, and the same
  questions work on any society. Nib's map note is made up. The hook's claim
  (most people in China live in the east, on the plains and along rivers) is
  general and safe to discuss with an atlas.


  Relevant ACARA AC9HH7K09 elaborations (examples, not a checklist): "examining
  the role of climate in enabling the establishment and expansion of agriculture
  around the Yellow River and how this supported the ancient society";
  "explaining the role of topography in providing barriers of defence for
  city-states, such as the surrounding seas, mountain ranges and river systems";
  "explaining how the Nile River enabled the establishment of ancient Egyptian
  society through farming (including the role of the inundation),
  transportation, defence (for example, the cataract fortifications) and
  religion". The Nile elaboration's religion part belongs with beliefs
  (AC9HH7K11), so the typical step leaves it out.


  First Nations: AC9HH7K09's elaborations have no First Nations content, and
  this course writes none. Deep time Australia (AC9HH7K02 to K07) stays a
  pointer page to First Nations-led resources.
running:
  - "Predict: ask for votes, then ask what the desert lacks."
  - "Try: after the match, ask students to point to each feature on the map."
  - "Worked example: let Nib's mistake sit before explaining it. Ask: 'Could the
    same cities have grown in the Gobi?'"
  - "Vary: compare the two climate labels on the map before the question."
  - "Make: students write in their own book; a partner gives feedback."
stuck:
  - see: A student lists features (Yellow River, Gobi, mountains) but says nothing
      about what they did.
    ask: What did that river give people? What did that desert stop them doing?
    fix: "Each feature needs a 'so what': water, soil, protection, or a limit."
  - see: A student says the rivers were good because they were safe.
    ask: What happens when the Yellow River floods?
    fix: Rivers gave water and soil, but floods were a danger. Lesson 3 comes back
      to this.
  - see: A student says the Qin heartland was chosen because it was near the sea.
    ask: Where is the Wei valley on the map, and where is the sea?
    fix: "The heartland was inland: river water, farmland and mountains around it."
support: Give pairs three cards (Yellow River, loess soil, Gobi) and ask for one
  'gave people' or 'got in their way' sentence each before the full map.
stretch: Why might a society on a big river and a society in small mountain
  valleys (China and Greece) end up organised so differently? What else, besides
  geography, would you want to know?
leads: Continue to From farming to cities.
exit:
  q: Name one feature of the land of ancient China, what it gave people or how it
    got in their way, and why that matters for where people lived.
  a: "For example: the Yellow River gave water and fresh soil, so farming villages
    and later cities grew along it; the Gobi was too dry to farm, so few people
    settled there."
explain: "Where an ancient society grew depended on its land: rivers and plains
  gave water and soil for farming, while deserts and mountains limited farming
  and travel but could protect a heartland."
sources:
  - title: "Britannica: Yellow River"
    url: https://www.britannica.com/place/Yellow-River
    checked: 2026-11-01
  - title: Zhang et al. (2012), Early mixed farming of millet and rice 7800 years
      ago in the middle Yellow River region, PLoS ONE
    url: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3524165
    checked: 2026-11-01
class:
  inquiry:
    q: If you had to start a farming village 7,000 years ago somewhere on this map,
      where would you put it, and why there?
    prompts:
      - What does your spot give you that other places do not?
      - What might go wrong there?
    notes: Most will choose a river or plain. Push for the reason (water, soil,
      protection), and bank 'what might go wrong' for lesson 3.
  activities:
    - at: run
      kind: activity
      title: Point and explain
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Project the map. Point to one feature at a time; pairs say one thing it
        gave people or one way it got in their way.
      notes: Accept 'both' answers for rivers (water, but floods). That is lesson 3's
        idea arriving early.
  questions:
    - at: make
      title: Check before moving on
      type: question
      q: Why could the Wei River valley support a capital, when the Gobi Desert could
        not?
      options:
        - The valley had river water and farmland; the desert had neither
        - The desert was too far from the sea for trade by ship
        - The valley never flooded, so crops were always safe
      answer: 0
      explain: Water and farmland fed a large population. A desert could not.
      feedback:
        - null
        - The valley was inland too. Water and soil are the difference.
        - Rivers do flood. The difference is water and soil.
```

# region: nib
The Qin capital was in the Wei River valley, a branch of the Yellow River.
The valley had river water, good soil, and mountains and passes around it.
Nib says: "The rivers and mountains just happened to be nearby. The Qin could have built the same cities anywhere."
Nib says: "So the land doesn't help explain where people lived."
